mainTopic: Which animals have בכור status: the source that excludes horses and camels, offspring that look like a different species, and the rule that kosher status follows the mother
overview: The amud finishes a proof that among non-kosher animals only a donkey has בכור status. The proof is that the Torah repeats ״פטר חמור״ word for word. רב אחאי challenges it: the second verse might only stop horses and camels from being redeemed with a lamb. The גמרא answers that a simple ״חמור״ would have been enough for that, so the exact repetition excludes them completely. Our תנא uses that repetition for another lesson, so רב פפא gives him a different source: the כלל ופרט of ״כל מקנך… שור ושה וחמור״. The רבנן and רבי יוסי הגלילי then argue over whether the donkey really belongs in that list, because of the words ״פטר״ and וי״ו. Next the גמרא asks a chain of questions about a mother that gives birth to a baby that looks like another species but has some of the mother's features. A ברייתא shows that a cow's donkey-like calf with some cow features is a בכור, while the horse-like cases stay undecided. Finally, the גמרא explains that the משנה's line ״שהיוצא״ is a memory aid: an animal's kosher status follows its mother. It then begins bringing a ברייתא as the source for that rule.

steps.title: The double phrase 'firstborn of a donkey' excludes horses and camels
steps.stepSummary: The Torah writes ״פטר חמור״ two times. The extra mention teaches that only donkeys have בכור status, not horses or camels.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'firstborn of a donkey' and again 'firstborn of a donkey,' two times. This teaches: I told you about firstborn donkeys, not firstborn horses and camels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse to prove that, among non-kosher animals, only a donkey has firstborn holiness. The proof is that the Torah repeats the phrase ״פטר חמור״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah mentions ״פטר חמור״ once in שמות פרק י״ג and once in שמות פרק ל״ד. Since nothing in the Torah is extra, the repetition must teach something. It teaches a limit: the law applies only to donkeys, not to other non-kosher animals like horses and camels.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The verse teaches us' – the formula that introduces a proof from a פסוק
The firstborn male donkey, which must be redeemed
Two times – the repetition that the proof is built on
Horses and camels – other non-kosher animals

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the halachic bottom line. A firstborn horse or camel has no בכור obligation at all. Only a donkey does.

phrases.english: The verse states: 'Firstborn of a donkey'
'firstborn of a donkey' – two times
I told you about firstborns of donkeys,
and not about firstborns of horses and camels.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר״ ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר״ שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the source derivation that began on the previous amud
steps.raayaObject: Only donkeys, not horses or camels, have בכור status
steps.raayaSupportSource: The repetition of ״פטר חמור״ in the Torah

steps.title: רב אחאי: one verse alone might have extended lamb-redemption to all animals
steps.stepSummary: רב אחאי begins his challenge. With only one verse, we would apply דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא ללמד and conclude that every non-kosher animal is redeemed with a lamb.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחאי challenges: If the Torah had written it only once, I would have said: something that was part of a general group and was taken out of it to teach a law does not teach only about itself. It teaches about the whole group. So all non-kosher animals would be redeemed with a lamb.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחאי starts to attack the proof. In this step he is setting up his challenge by explaining what we would have thought if there were only one verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule of דרשה: when one item is singled out from a group to teach a law, that law applies to the whole group. Here, the donkey is one of the non-kosher animals, and it was singled out to be redeemed with a lamb. So with only one verse, we would say all non-kosher animals are redeemed with a lamb. רב אחאי is laying the groundwork to show that the second verse may be needed just to block this.

keyTerms.meaning: Challenges, refutes
'The Merciful One' – a name for God as the Author of the Torah

keyTerms.term: דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה בַּכְּלָל וְיָצָא מִן הַכְּלָל לְלַמֵּד
keyTerms.meaning: An item that was part of a general group and was singled out to teach a law
It was not singled out to teach only about itself, but about the whole group
'And really' – introduces the actual result being argued for

steps.confusionAlert: רב אחאי does not hold that horses really need redemption with a lamb. He is explaining why a second verse would be necessary even if it does not teach the exclusion from בכור status.

phrases.english: Rav Achai challenges:
If the Merciful One had written it once,
I would have said: an item that was included in a generalization,
and emerged from the generalization to teach,
did not emerge to teach about itself alone

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְלַמֵּד עַל הַכְּלָל כּוּלּוֹ יָצָא,
phrases.english: but emerged to teach about the entire generalization,
and so really, all would be redeemed with a lamb.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּרֵיךְ רַב אַחַאי: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא חַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the challenge to the proof from repetition
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the second ״פטר חמור״ teaches exclusion from בכור status
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second verse might be needed for a different purpose: to block the rule of דבר שהיה בכלל ויצא from applying

steps.title: Maybe the second verse only excludes horses and camels from redemption with a lamb
steps.stepSummary: רב אחאי finishes his challenge. The second verse may only teach that horses and camels are not redeemed with a lamb. They might still need redemption with any other item.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the Merciful One wrote 'firstborn of a donkey' another time to teach: donkeys, and not horses and camels. But you could say the verse only excludes them from a lamb, and really they must be redeemed with anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחאי delivers the punch of his challenge. The second verse might exclude horses and camels only from the lamb, not from בכור status altogether.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 used the extra verse to say horses and camels have no firstborn holiness at all. רב אחאי offers a smaller reading: the verse cancels only the lamb requirement that דבר שהיה בכלל would have created. If that is right, horses and camels might still be holy and need redemption with some other item, so the original proof falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Another (one), a second time
'But I could say' – introduces an alternative reading
He excluded them
With any item

phrases.english: So the Merciful One wrote 'firstborn of a donkey' another time,

phrases.aramaic: פִּטְרֵי חֲמוֹרִים וְלֹא פִּטְרֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים,
phrases.english: to teach firstborn donkeys and not firstborn horses and camels,
but I could say: it excluded them from redemption with a lamb,
but really they are redeemed with any item!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא: מַעֲטִינְהוּ מִשֶׂה, וּלְעוֹלָם בְּכׇל דָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge that step 2 set up
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof in step 1 that horses and camels have no בכור status
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second verse can be fully explained as excluding only lamb-redemption, so it does not prove a complete exclusion from בכור status

steps.title: The identical wording of both verses proves a complete exclusion
steps.stepSummary: If the goal were only to block the lamb, the Torah could have written the second verse as ״חמור תפדה בשה״. Repeating the exact phrase ״פטר חמור״ shows that horses and camels have no בכור status at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the Merciful One write 'Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb' and 'A donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.' Why do I need 'firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb' written the same way both times? To teach: I told you about firstborn donkeys, and not firstborn horses and camels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב אחאי by pointing to the exact wording of the verse. The word ״פטר״ appears in both verses, which shows the repetition is teaching something more than just blocking the lamb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To block דבר שהיה בכלל, a second verse that said only ״חמור״ would have been enough. The Torah instead repeated the full phrase ״פטר חמור״, so the extra word must teach that only a donkey's firstborn is holy. That means horses and camels are excluded from בכור status entirely, which restores the proof from step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: If so – introduces a rebuttal showing what the Torah would have written
You shall redeem with a lamb
Why do I need it? – points to extra wording that must teach something

steps.whatToRemember: Only a firstborn donkey has בכור status among non-kosher animals. The proof is that the Torah repeats the exact phrase ״פטר חמור״. A simple ״חמור״ would have been enough just to block דבר שהיה בכלל, so the full repetition teaches a complete exclusion of horses and camels.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a classic method of the גמרא: proving what a verse teaches from how the Torah could have phrased it differently.

phrases.english: If so, let the Merciful One write:
'Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb'
and 'A donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.'
'Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,'
'firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb' – why do I need both?
I told you about firstborns of donkeys,
and not about firstborns of horses and camels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחאי's challenge and restores the proof from step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precision of wording: the Torah could have phrased the verse more briefly
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second verse only excludes horses and camels from redemption with a lamb
steps.terutzMaskana: The exact repetition of ״פטר חמור״ shows a complete exclusion of horses and camels from בכור status

steps.title: How does our תנא exclude horses and camels?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the תנא of our משנה learns that horses and camels have no בכור status, since he uses the double ״פטר חמור״ for something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא, where does he learn that horses and camels are excluded?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the תנא of our משנה and asks for his source that horses and camels are not included in בכור. This question sets up רב פפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 1–4 used the double ״פטר חמור״ to exclude horses and camels. Our תנא already uses that repetition to teach that both the mother and the baby must be donkeys. So that verse is "taken" for him, and he needs a different source.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא of our own משנה
To exclude
Horses and camels
From where does he know it? (asking for a source)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree that horses and camels have no בכור status. The only question is which verse each side uses to learn it.

phrases.english: And our Tanna (of the Mishnah),
phrases.notes: He uses the double ״פטר חמור״ to teach that both mother and baby must be donkeys.

phrases.english: to exclude horses and camels — from where does he learn it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא דִידַן, לְמַעוֹטֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים, מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing how the other opinion learns the exclusion from the double ״פטר חמור״, the גמרא asks about the תנא who uses that verse differently.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source the תנא of our משנה uses to exclude horses and camels from בכור status.

steps.title: רב פפא learns it from a general statement followed by a list
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says ״כל מקנך״ is a general statement and ״שור ושה וחמור״ is the list. By the rule of כלל ופרט, only the listed animals are included.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: "All your livestock" is a general statement. "Ox, sheep, and donkey" is the detail. When a general statement is followed by a detail, the general includes only what is in the detail. So ox, sheep, and donkey are included, and nothing else is.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question using the rule of כלל ופרט. The broad words "all your livestock" are limited by the specific animals listed after them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally "all your livestock" would include every animal, horses and camels too. But the Torah then lists ox, sheep, and donkey, and when a general phrase is followed by a list, the list limits it. So בכור applies only to those three animals, and horses and camels are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Stated a general category
Listed specific details
A rule of Torah interpretation: a general statement followed by details
The general includes only what is in the detail
Your livestock

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the תנא of our משנה a full source for the exclusion. That leaves the double ״פטר חמור״ free for his own lesson about mother and baby.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
"All your livestock, the males" — this is a general statement,
"ox and sheep and donkey" — this is a detail (a specific list),
a general statement followed by a detail —
the general includes only what is in the detail,
ox, sheep, and donkey — yes (they have בכור status),
anything else — no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כׇּל מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר — כָּלַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Horses and camels are excluded through the כלל ופרט of ״כל מקנך״ followed by ״שור ושה וחמור״.

steps.title: Why רבי יוסי הגלילי does not use this list
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יוסי הגלילי does not use רב פפא's source. It answers that the word ״פטר״ in ״ופטר חמור״ breaks off the donkey from the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי הגלילי? The word "firstborn" interrupts the topic.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יוסי הגלילי needs the double ״פטר חמור״ if a כלל ופרט is available. It answers that, in his reading, the donkey is not part of the list at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says ״שור ושה״ and then begins again with ״ופטר חמור״. רבי יוסי הגלילי reads the new word ״פטר״ as the start of a separate topic. So the donkey is not one of the details limiting ״כל מקנך״, and this כלל ופרט cannot teach that donkeys are the only non-kosher animal with בכור status.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn (literally, "that which opens the womb")
It interrupted the topic

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (why doesn't he learn it this way)?
The word "firstborn" (in "and the firstborn of a donkey") interrupts the topic,
phrases.notes: So the donkey is not part of the list attached to ״כל מקנך״.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the other opinion does not accept רב פפא's derivation.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual reading: the word ״פטר״ separates the donkey from the list.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a כלל ופרט is available, רבי יוסי הגלילי should not need the double ״פטר חמור״.
steps.terutzMaskana: For him the donkey is a separate topic, so the כלל ופרט does not do the job, and he needs the extra verse.

steps.title: The רבנן: the letter וי״ו joins the donkey back in
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן answer that the וי״ו in ״ופטר חמור״ ("and") connects the donkey back to the list of ox and sheep.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? The letter וי״ו ("and") brings it back, and the verse joins it together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the רבנן (our תנא) answer the claim that ״פטר״ breaks the list. They point to the small word "and" at the start of ״ופטר חמור״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״ופטר״ begins with וי״ו, which means "and". "And" connects what comes after it to what came before. So even though ״פטר״ might look like a break, the וי״ו pulls the donkey back into the same list, and the כלל ופרט works.

keyTerms.meaning: The letter ו, meaning "and" — it connects words together
The verse goes back and combines it
The Sages (here, the view of our תנא)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis (how do they answer this)?
The letter vav ("and") — the verse comes back and joins it (to the list).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the claim from step 7 that ״פטר״ separates the donkey from the list.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading that the donkey is cut off from the list.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It ignores the וי״ו, which connects the donkey back to ox and sheep.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי: if it belonged in the list, neither word would be written
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי הגלילי replies that if the donkey were part of the list, the Torah would have written neither the וי״ו nor ״פטר״. It would simply say "ox, sheep, donkey".
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוסי הגלילי? Let the Torah write neither the וי״ו nor "firstborn".
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי הגלילי answers the רבנן's argument about the וי״ו. He says that adding these extra words shows the donkey is a new topic, not part of the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah wanted the donkey in the list, the simplest wording would be to name it right after ox and sheep, with no ״ו״ and no ״פטר״. Since the Torah added the word ״פטר״, the break is real, and the וי״ו alone does not undo it. So for him the donkey stays separate, and he needs the double ״פטר חמור״ to exclude horses and camels.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it not write (the Torah should have left it out)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that horses and camels have no בכור status. Our תנא learns it from the כלל ופרט of ״כל מקנך… שור ושה וחמור״, because the וי״ו joins the donkey into the list. רבי יוסי הגלילי says ״פטר״ separates the donkey from the list, so he learns the exclusion from the repeated ״פטר חמור״.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (how does he respond)?
Let it write neither the vav nor "firstborn" (if the donkey were really part of the list).
phrases.notes: Writing ״פטר״ again shows a new topic has started.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי? לָא לִכְתּוֹב לָא וָי״ו וְלָא ״פֶּטֶר״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the רבנן's וי״ו argument from step 8 and keeps רבי יוסי הגלילי's reading from step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the וי״ו joins the donkey into the list.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If the donkey belonged in the list, the Torah would not have written the extra words at all. Writing ״פטר״ shows a real break.

steps.title: The רבנן explain why the Torah separates the donkey and then joins it back
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן answer רבי יוסי הגלילי. The Torah wrote ״פטר״ to separate the donkey from the ox and sheep, because its holiness is different. Then it wrote the וי״ו to join the donkey back into the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, how do they answer? A firstborn donkey has קדושת דמים (holiness of value), while an ox and sheep have קדושת הגוף (holiness of the body itself). So the Torah separates them, and then joins them back together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the רבנן answer רבי יוסי הגלילי's point from Step 9, and gives their answer. They explain why both ״פטר״ and the וי״ו are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי הגלילי said that if the donkey were part of the list, the Torah would not need ״פטר״ or the וי״ו. The רבנן reply that ״פטר״ marks a real difference: a firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb, while a firstborn ox or sheep is brought on the מזבח. The וי״ו still keeps the donkey inside the list, so the כלל ופרט of רב פפא stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / because
Holiness of value — the animal itself is not offered; its value goes to holiness (the donkey is redeemed with a lamb)
Holiness of the body — the animal itself is holy and is brought as a קרבן (ox, sheep)
Separates / cuts off
Mixes / joins together

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן keep the donkey in the list. ״פטר״ only shows that the donkey's kind of holiness is different, and the וי״ו brings it back into the list. So horses and camels stay excluded through the כלל ופרט.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis? (How do they answer this?)
Since this one (the donkey) has holiness of value,
and that one (ox and sheep) has holiness of the body —
the verse separates them, and then joins them back together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוסי הגלילי's argument from Step 9 that the extra words show the donkey is cut off from the list.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why each extra word in the verse is needed (one separates, one rejoins)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words ״פטר״ and the וי״ו seem extra if the donkey is simply part of the list.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״פטר״ shows the difference in holiness (קדושת דמים vs. קדושת הגוף), and the וי״ו still includes the donkey in the list.

steps.title: New question: a cow gave birth to a donkey-like calf with some cow features
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks a new question. What is the law when a cow gives birth to a calf that looks like a donkey but has some of the cow's features?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: a cow gave birth to something like a donkey, and it has some of the cow's features. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new question (איבעיא להו). The next steps will explain why the question is hard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that a donkey-like calf born to a cow is not a בכור. The new question is narrower: what if the calf still has some features of its mother? Does that partial resemblance give it בכור status?

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them (the opening of a בעיא)
Something like a donkey (it looks like a donkey)
Some identifying features (of the mother)
What is the law?

phrases.english: A question was asked among them:
A cow that gave birth to something like a donkey,
and it has some (of the mother's) features — what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the verse discussion and opens a new practical question about mixed-looking offspring.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a donkey-like calf born to a cow have בכור status if it has some of the cow's features?

steps.title: The known case: goat and sheep offspring with some of the mother's features
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the known rule as a comparison. A goat that gave birth to a sheep-like kid, or a sheep that gave birth to a goat-like lamb, is a בכור if it has some of the mother's features. That may be because both animals are טהורה and both have קדושת הגוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: A goat that gave birth to something like a sheep, or a sheep that gave birth to something like a goat: when it has some of the mother's features, it is a בכור. That is because both are kosher animals, and both have holiness of the body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the question by quoting a case where the law is already known. The next step will show why our case might be different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the goat/sheep case, partial resemblance is enough for בכור status. But the reason may be that the two animals are very alike: both are טהורה and both are offered on the מזבח. This is the 'similar animals' side of the comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: Goat
Ewe / sheep
Is obligated in the law of בכור (has firstborn status)
A kosher (pure) animal

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the answer to the question. It is the known case that the גמרא compares against. The point is to show why the goat/sheep case may be easier than the cow/donkey case.

phrases.english: A goat that gave birth to something like a sheep,
and a sheep that gave birth to something like a goat,
that when it has some (of the mother's) features —
it is obligated in the law of firstborn,
because this one is kosher and that one is kosher,

phrases.aramaic: הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף.
phrases.english: this one has holiness of the body and that one has holiness of the body.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֵז שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין רָחֵל, וְרָחֵל שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין עֵז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the question by bringing the known goat/sheep case as a comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Goat/sheep offspring with some of the mother's features is a בכור, possibly because the two animals share purity and קדושת הגוף.

steps.title: The two sides: different holiness, or both animals have firstborn status
steps.stepSummary: Side one: a cow and a donkey are very different (טהורה vs. טמאה, קדושת הגוף vs. קדושת דמים), so the calf is not a בכור. Side two: both cow and donkey have בכור status, so the calf is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, one is non-kosher and one is kosher. One has holiness of the body and one has holiness of value. So maybe it is not a בכור. Or perhaps, since both kinds of animals become holy as a בכור, it is holy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out both sides of the question. The ברייתא brought in step 18 answers it, as step 19 explains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the cow and donkey are too different, unlike goat and sheep, so partial resemblance does not help. Side two: what matters is only that both species have בכור laws, and a donkey does have בכור status through פטר חמור. The question is whether the kind of holiness must match, or only the fact that both have בכור status.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-kosher animal
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of the question)
This one and that one — both
Able to be made holy

steps.whyThisMatters: This question rests on the difference between קדושת הגוף and קדושת דמים. A cow and a donkey both have בכור status, but with different kinds of holiness, and that is exactly what makes this question possible.

phrases.english: Here, where this one is non-kosher and that one is kosher,

phrases.aramaic: הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים — לָא,
phrases.english: this one has holiness of the body and that one holiness of value — perhaps not (a firstborn),
or perhaps: since both this one and that one
can become holy as a firstborn — it is holy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the cow/donkey case with the goat/sheep case and presents both possible sides.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does בכור status need the two species to share the same type of holiness and purity, or is it enough that both species have בכור laws?

steps.title: A donkey that gives birth to a horse-like foal
steps.stepSummary: If a cow's donkey-like calf is holy because both cow and donkey have בכור status, what about a donkey that gives birth to a horse-like foal? A horse has no בכור status at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that since both (cow and donkey) are subject to בכור holiness, the calf is holy, then what about a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal? Here, a horse is certainly not subject to בכור holiness. Or perhaps, since it is also a non-kosher species like its mother, it is holy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא assumes, just for argument, that the last question is answered 'yes, holy.' Then it asks a harder follow-up case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the cow-to-donkey case, the reason to say 'holy' was that both animals have בכור status. A horse has no בכור status, so that reason disappears here. But a new reason may take its place: the donkey and the horse are both טמאה animals, so they are more alike.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (assuming the previous question is answered a certain way)
A horse-like animal (an offspring that looks like a horse)
Something that can become holy as a בכור
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question)
A non-kosher species

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'אם תמצי לומר' does not mean the earlier question was answered. It only means: IF it is answered 'holy,' here is the next question.

phrases.english: And if you say:
since this one and that one (cow and donkey)
are sanctified with firstborn status, it is holy,
phrases.notes: This assumes the answer to the question in step 13.

phrases.english: what about a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like animal?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי לָא בַּת מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה הוּא,
phrases.english: Here it certainly is not something that becomes holy as a firstborn,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּמִין טְמֵאָה הוּא קָדוֹשׁ?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since it is a non-kosher species (like its mother), it is holy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a harder follow-up case on top of the question in steps 11 and 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a donkey's horse-like foal with some of its mother's features count as a בכור?

steps.title: A cow that gives birth to a horse-like calf
steps.stepSummary: If even the donkey's horse-like foal is holy, what about a cow that gives birth to a horse-like calf? These two animals differ in every way. Or perhaps sharing some of the mother's features is what really counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that since it is a non-kosher species it is holy, then what about a cow that gave birth to a horse-like calf? Here, this one is kosher and that one is not. This one can be holy as a בכור and that one cannot. Or perhaps having the mother's features is a significant thing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again assumes the last question is answered 'holy.' Then it asks the most extreme case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cow and horse share nothing. One is טהורה and one is טמאה. One has בכור status and one does not. So neither reason from the earlier cases applies. The only remaining reason to call the calf holy is that the mother's features (סימנין) are important on their own.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a second level of assumption)
This one... and that one... (contrasting two things)
Physical features or signs (here, features of the mother)
It is a significant matter; it counts

phrases.english: If you say:
since it is a non-kosher species, it is holy,
phrases.notes: This assumes the answer to step 14.

phrases.english: what about a cow that gave birth to a horse-like animal?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי הָא טְהוֹרָה וְהָא טְמֵאָה,
phrases.english: Here certainly, this one is kosher and that one is non-kosher,
this one can become holy as a firstborn
and that one cannot become holy as a firstborn,
or perhaps the (mother's) features are a significant matter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a third, most extreme case on top of step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a cow's horse-like calf with some of its mother's features count as a בכור? In other words, do the mother's סימנין count even when the two species share nothing?

steps.title: First proof attempt: a kosher animal giving birth to a non-kosher-looking one
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that a kosher animal giving birth to a non-kosher-looking one is exempt, but if the offspring has some of the mother's features, it is a בכור. The גמרא suggests this includes even a cow giving birth to a horse-like calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher-looking animal is exempt from בכור. If the offspring has some of the mother's features, it is obligated in בכור. Doesn't this include even a cow that gave birth to a horse-like calf?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the hardest question, from step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא speaks broadly about any 'non-kosher animal,' without naming a species. That wording seems to include a horse-like calf too. If so, the mother's features alone are enough to make the calf a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source brought as proof)
Exempt from בכור status
Some of the features (of the mother)
Obligated in בכור status (the offspring is a בכור)
Is it not that...? (proposes how to read a source)

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: בְּהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה —
phrases.english: a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher-looking animal —
is exempt from firstborn status;
if it has some of the (mother's) features —
it is obligated in firstborn status.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו אֲפִילּוּ פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס?
phrases.english: Is it not (saying this) even about a cow that gave birth to a horse-like animal?
phrases.notes: The general wording 'non-kosher animal' would seem to include a horse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That a cow's horse-like calf with some of its mother's features is a בכור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that uses the general wording 'a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher-looking animal.'

steps.title: The proof is limited to a donkey-like calf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The ברייתא may only be talking about a cow giving birth to a donkey-like calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the proof from step 16. It says the ברייתא could be talking about a narrower case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'non-kosher animal' in the ברייתא could just mean a donkey. A donkey at least has בכור status like the cow. So the ברייתא tells us nothing about a horse-like calf, and the question in step 15 stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: No (a rejection of the suggested reading)
A donkey-like animal
A firstborn donkey, which has בכור status

phrases.english: No, (it means) a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The ברייתא is limited to the cow-to-donkey case, so it proves nothing about a horse-like calf.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the general word 'non-kosher' must include a horse. It can just as easily mean only a donkey.

steps.title: Second proof attempt: a ברייתא that lists both cases
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא names two cases: a cow giving birth to a donkey-like calf, and a donkey giving birth to a horse-like foal. It says the offspring is a בכור if it has some of the mother's features. The גמרא suggests this last clause applies to both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf, and a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal, are exempt from בכור. If the offspring has some of the mother's features, it is obligated in בכור. Doesn't this apply to both?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא to try to answer the question from step 14, the donkey's horse-like foal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא names the donkey-to-horse case outright. If the rule 'some features means it is a בכור' covers both cases, then the question in step 14 is answered: the foal is holy.

keyTerms.meaning: On both of them (the rule applies to both cases)
A teaching of the תנאים that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: Come and hear:
a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like animal,
and a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like animal —
are exempt from firstborn status;
if it has some of the (mother's) features —
it is obligated in firstborn status.
Is it not (saying this) about both?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof fails, the גמרא tries a new source aimed at the question in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That a donkey's horse-like foal with some of its mother's features is a בכור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that lists both the cow-to-donkey case and the donkey-to-horse case before stating the 'some features' rule.

steps.title: The rule applies only to the cow's donkey-like calf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The 'some features' clause may refer only to the cow giving birth to a donkey-like calf, not to the donkey giving birth to a horse-like foal.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is about the cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back the second proof. The last clause of the ברייתא may refer to only one of its two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'if it has some features, it is a בכור' may apply only to the first case. If so, the ברייתא says nothing about a donkey's horse-like foal that has some of its mother's features. Either way, the ברייתא clearly answers the original question from step 11: a cow's donkey-like calf with some of its mother's features is a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: No (Aramaic form of the rejection)
Short for עַל, meaning 'about' or 'referring to'
The last clause of a teaching

steps.whatToRemember: Only one question gets answered here. A cow's donkey-like calf with some of its mother's features is a בכור. The donkey-to-horse case and the cow-to-horse case remain open.
steps.confusionAlert: Even though this proof is pushed back, the ברייתא still answers the original question about a cow's donkey-like calf. Only the horse-like cases stay unanswered.

phrases.english: No, (it refers) to the cow that gave birth to a donkey-like animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The 'some features' clause is limited to the cow-to-donkey case, so the donkey-to-horse question stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the last clause covers every case listed before it. It may cover only the first case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A cow's donkey-like calf with some of its mother's features is a בכור. The horse-like cases are not settled.

steps.title: Why mention the donkey with a horse-like foal at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the 'some features' clause covers only the cow case, the donkey-horse case seems to teach nothing new. Its exemption already follows from the cow case.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, the donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal: why does the ברייתא teach it? To say it is exempt? That is obvious! Look at the cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf. Both a cow and a donkey can have בכורה holiness, and still you said: if the calf has some of the mother's features, yes, it is a בכור, and if not, no. So for a donkey giving birth to a horse-like foal, do we even need to be told?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the reading from step 19. If the 'some features' clause is not about the donkey-horse case, then that case seems to have no purpose in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the cow case, both the mother's species and the calf's look-alike species can carry בכורה holiness. Even so, the calf is exempt unless it has some of the mother's features. A horse can never carry בכורה holiness, so a horse-like foal should be exempt all the more. Teaching it looks pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: to exempt, i.e. to teach that it is not a בכור
it is obvious
species that can become holy as a בכור
is it even necessary to say?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not lose track of the cow case. A cow and a donkey can both be a בכור: a cow as a sacrifice, and a donkey through פטר חמור, its redemption. A horse can never be one. That is why the horse case looks 'even more obvious.'

phrases.english: But a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal,
for what purpose does it teach it?
To exempt it? That is obvious!

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא, וּמָה פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר,
phrases.english: Now, if a cow that gave birth to a donkey-like calf,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּנֵי מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה נִינְהוּ,
phrases.english: where both this and that can become holy as a firstborn,

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרַתְּ: אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — אִין,
phrases.english: you said: if it has some of the mother's features, yes,
and if not, no,
then a donkey that gave birth to a horse-like foal, is it even necessary to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל חֲמוֹר שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס, לְמַאי קָתָנֵי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of the ברייתא proposed in the דחיה of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the 'some features' clause covers only the cow-donkey case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On that reading, the donkey-horse case can only be teaching an exemption. That exemption already follows by קל וחומר from the cow case, so the case would be superfluous.

steps.title: The case is needed because a donkey and a horse look alike
steps.stepSummary: A donkey and a horse share features, so one might think the foal is just a red donkey and is holy. The ברייתא teaches that it is still exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed. You might have thought this: there, in the cow case, the cow has horns and the donkey has none. The cow's hooves are split and the donkey's are closed. That is why the calf is exempt. But here, neither the donkey nor the horse has horns, and both have closed hooves. So I might say the foal is just a red donkey. The ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the reading from step 19. It explains why the donkey-horse case teaches something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר from step 20 only works if the two cases are alike. They are not. A cow and a donkey are completely different, but a donkey and a horse share key features. So we might treat the horse-like foal as a donkey of unusual color, a 'red donkey.' The ברייתא tells us it counts as a different kind and is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: it was needed
it might have entered your mind
its hooves are split
its hooves are closed (not split)
a red donkey, i.e. a donkey that simply has a horse's coloring
it teaches us (otherwise)

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא lists the donkey-horse case because a donkey and a horse look so alike. The case teaches that a horse-like foal born to a donkey, without the mother's features, is still a different kind and is not a בכור. So the reading from step 19 holds, and the question about a foal that does have some of the mother's features stays unresolved.

phrases.english: It was needed. It might enter your mind:
There, it is because this one (the cow) has horns,
and this one (the donkey) does not have horns;
this one's hooves are split,
and that one's hooves are closed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי אֵין לָהּ קַרְנַיִם,
phrases.english: But here, where both this and that have no horns,
and both this and that have closed hooves,
I might say it is merely a red donkey,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 by showing the donkey-horse case is not obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Breaking the קל וחומר by pointing to a key difference: a donkey and a horse look alike, while a cow and a donkey do not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because a donkey and a horse share features (no horns, closed hooves), the foal might be seen as a red donkey and treated as a בכור.
steps.terutzMaskana: The horse-like foal is a different kind and is exempt from בכורה.

steps.title: Why does the משנה add the reason 'because what comes out'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's rule about eating such animals. It asks why the משנה needed to add the closing reason 'שהיוצא.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And what is their law for eating, and so on.' Why do I need the משנה to teach 'because what comes out'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes the משנה's rule about eating an animal that looks like another species and questions its wording. The answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already gave the rulings for eating. The offspring of a kosher animal may be eaten, and the offspring of a non-kosher animal may not. Then it adds the reason: what comes out of the non-kosher animal is non-kosher, and what comes out of the kosher animal is kosher. The גמרא asks what that extra line teaches beyond the rulings themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: regarding eating (whether it is kosher to eat)
why do I need it to teach?
because what comes out (from the animal)

phrases.english: The משנה said: "And what is their status for eating, etc."
Why do I need it to teach "because what comes out"?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה הֵן בַּאֲכִילָה כּוּ׳. לְמָה לִי לְמִיתְנֵי ״שֶׁהַיּוֹצֵא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the בכורה discussion and opens a new topic on the משנה's rule about eating.
steps.kashyaTarget: The closing phrase of the משנה: 'שהיוצא מן הטמא טמא והיוצא מן הטהור טהור.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rulings about eating are already stated, so the added reason seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The closing reason is only a memory aid: follow the mother
steps.stepSummary: The phrase 'שהיוצא' adds no new law. It is a סימן so you don't mix up the two cases and judge the baby by its own looks. Its status follows its mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is just a memory aid, so the rule doesn't get switched in your mind. You should not say: 'Go by the baby's own appearance, so this one is fully kosher and that one is fully non-kosher.' Rather, go by its mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 22. The extra closing words in the משנה are a memory aid, not a new law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already gave both rulings. So the reason 'what comes from a טמא is טמא, and what comes from a טהור is טהור' looks extra. The גמרא says it is there so you will not flip the rules by judging from the baby's appearance. The key is always the mother.

keyTerms.meaning: Just a memory aid (mnemonic)
So that you don't mix it up
Go after its mother; the mother decides the status
Full, complete (here: fully kosher or fully non-kosher)

steps.whatToRemember: An animal's kosher status follows its mother, not its own looks. The משנה's closing reason is just a reminder of this.

phrases.english: It is merely a memory aid,
so that it does not get switched for you,
so that you should not say:
go after its own (appearance),
and this one is a fully kosher animal,
phrases.notes: The kosher-looking baby of a non-kosher mother.

phrases.english: and that one is a fully non-kosher animal,
phrases.notes: The non-kosher-looking baby of a kosher mother.

phrases.english: rather, go after its mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 22 about why 'שהיוצא' was needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra wording is a memory aid, not new law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might judge the baby by its own signs and so reverse the rulings.
steps.terutzMaskana: The reason is added only as a reminder to follow the mother.

steps.title: Where do we learn this rule from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the rule that status follows the mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the Torah source of the rule that the mother decides. This sets up the ברייתא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the rule is clear, the גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches it. This is a request for a source, not an attack.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things learned? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the rule is clarified, the גמרא asks for its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that teaches that an animal's status follows its mother.

steps.title: A ברייתא reads the verse as forbidding a kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from ״אַךְ אֶת זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ״ that some animals chew the cud and have split hooves, yet are forbidden. This is a טהור born from a טמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'But this you shall not eat, of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof.' This means there is an animal that chews the cud and splits the hoof, yet you may not eat it. Which one is that? A kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. It reads the פסוק as forbidding an animal with kosher signs that was born from a non-kosher mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the פסוק as if it says: 'Even among those that have the kosher signs, there is one you may not eat.' The only such animal is a kosher-looking baby of a טמא mother. This supports the rule that the mother decides.

keyTerms.meaning: Chews the cud (a kosher sign)
Has a split hoof (a kosher sign)
A kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother
As the רבנן taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"But this you shall not eat
of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof"
you have one that chews the cud
and has split hooves, yet you may not eat it.
And which is this?
A kosher-looking animal that was born from a non-kosher one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source requested in Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק ״אַךְ אֶת זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה״ forbids a kosher-looking animal born from a non-kosher mother.

steps.title: Maybe the verse forbids a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher mother
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises another reading. Perhaps the פסוק forbids a non-kosher-looking baby born from a kosher mother. It then asks how 'from those that chew the cud' would fit that reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps it means only a non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher one. Then what would 'of those that chew the cud and of those that split the hoof' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges its own reading by suggesting the opposite case. This sets up its next move, which comes in the following text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under this other reading, 'from those that chew the cud' would mean 'born from' kosher animals. Then the forbidden one would be a non-kosher-looking baby of a kosher mother. This would go against the משנה, which permits that baby. So the ברייתא must show why its first reading is right.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps it is only... (suggesting another reading)
A non-kosher-looking animal born from a kosher mother

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion inside the ברייתא, not the final law. The משנה rules that a non-kosher-looking baby of a kosher mother is permitted.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words could mean 'born from cud-chewers.' Then the forbidden animal would be a טמא born from a טהור, the opposite case.
